title: Quantifiers — Many, Much, A Lot Of, Few, Little
subtitle: Say how much or how many, and know which words go with which kind of noun.
objectives: Tell the difference between countable and uncountable nouns
Use many/much/a lot of for large quantities
Use a few/a little (enough) versus few/little (not enough)

content.intro: Some nouns can be counted one by one (books, friends); others can't (milk, patience). English uses different quantity words depending on which type you're talking about.

rules.heading: a) Large quantities
rules.body:
• many + countable plural noun: many books, many friends
  • much + uncountable noun: much milk, much time (mostly in questions/negatives)
  • a lot of + either: a lot of books, a lot of milk (works everywhere, most common in everyday speech)

rules.heading: b) Small quantities: enough vs. not enough
rules.body:
• a few (countable) / a little (uncountable) = a small amount, but enough: I have a few friends here. / There's a little milk left.
  • few (countable) / little (uncountable) = almost none, a negative feeling: I have few friends here. (= not enough, I'm a bit lonely) / There's little milk left. (= almost none, a problem)

examples: There are many books on the shelf.
Do you have much milk in the fridge?
There are a lot of people at the party.
I have a few questions before we start.
She has few friends in this city.

commonMistakes.wrong: There are much books on the shelf.
commonMistakes.right: There are many books on the shelf.

commonMistakes.why: "Money" is uncountable — use "a little," not "a few."

commonMistakes.wrong: She has a few friends, so she feels lonely.
commonMistakes.right: She has few friends, so she feels lonely.
commonMistakes.why: "A few" means a small but sufficient number; the negative feeling here needs "few" (not enough).

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with many, much, a few, or a little.

items.prompt: There are ___ books on the shelf.
Do you have ___ milk in the fridge?
items.explanation: "Milk" is uncountable — use "much" in this question.

items.prompt: I have ___ questions before we start.
items.explanation: "Questions" is countable, and this is a small but sufficient amount — "a few."

items.prompt: There's ___ time left, so let's hurry.
"There were ___ people at the party." — which word fits a large, general amount, in any style?
items.explanation: "A lot of" works with both countable and uncountable nouns and fits any style.

items.prompt: He didn't have ___ patience during the long meeting.
items.explanation: "Patience" is uncountable — "much" is correct, especially in this negative sentence.

items.incorrect: There are much people at the airport.
answer: There are many people at the airport.
There are a lot of people at the airport.
items.explanation: "People" is countable — use "many" or "a lot of," not "much."

items.incorrect: I have a few money for the trip.
answer: I have a little money for the trip.
items.explanation: "Money" is uncountable — use "a little," not "a few."

summary: Countable nouns (books, friends) → many / a few / few.
Uncountable nouns (milk, time, patience) → much / a little / little.
A lot of works with both, and is the most common choice in everyday speech.
A few/a little = a small but sufficient amount; few/little = almost none, often negative.
